The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

derivations.claim: Write the mean and covariance of $(U,V)$ in block form as $(m_U,m_V)$ and $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_U,\Sigma_V)$; the off-diagonal blocks vanish by hypothesis and each diagonal block is positive semidefinite as a principal block of $\Sigma$. Let $A_U,A_V$ be their positive-semidefinite square roots and put $A=\operatorname{diag}(A_U,A_V)$. Then $A$ is positive semidefinite, $A^2=\Sigma$, and [F2] identifies it with the unique positive-semidefinite square root of $\Sigma$.

By [F1], the joint law has a realization $(m_U+A_UW_U,m_V+A_VW_V)$ with independent standard-normal coordinates in $W_U,W_V$. By [F3] the full coordinate vector has product law, so rectangles in the two coordinate blocks factor into their block marginals; [F6] gives block independence. Applying [F4] to the separate block-affine maps preserves independence.

The realization in step 2.1 and the original vector have the same multivariate-normal law by [F5]. Their joint and marginal rectangle probabilities therefore agree; the factorization established in step 2.1 transfers to the original pair, and [F6] gives independence. AC is used only through the Gaussian-law construction and uniqueness suppliers.

citations.quote:
Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a weakly stationary real process and let
$n,h\ge1$. The affine $L^2$ minimization defining the finite-history best
linear forecast of $X_{n+h}$ from $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ has a unique minimizing
almost-sure class, even when the history covariance matrix is singular.

Let $X,Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be square-integrable real random variables on one
probability space, and write
$$W:=\operatorname{span}\big([1],[Y_1],\dots,[Y_n]\big)\subseteq L^2(\mathbb P),$$
where $[\cdot]$ denotes the almost-everywhere class from
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]].

Then there is a unique class $[Z_*]\in W$ minimizing $\|[X]-[Z]\|_2$ over
$[Z]\in W$. This minimizing class has an affine representative
$Z_*=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^n a_jY_j$, and its coefficients satisfy
$$a_0=\mathbb E[X]-\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\mathbb E[Y_j],$$
$$\sum_{j=1}^n \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)a_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y_i)\qquad(1\le i\le n).$$

The class $[Z_*]$ is unique. If the covariance matrix
$\Gamma=(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j))_{i,j}$ is singular, the coefficient vector
need not be uniquely determined by the normal equations, but any two solutions
yield the same predictor almost surely.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real-valued stochastic process on one
probability space, so each $X_t$ is a real random variable and each finite
tuple has its pushforward law
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]).
We call $X$ a **time series** here because its index set is $\mathbb Z$.

The process is **strictly stationary** when for every integer $r\ge1$, every
$t_1,\ldots,t_r\in\mathbb Z$, and every shift $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$\mathcal L(X_{t_1+m},\ldots,X_{t_r+m})=\mathcal L(X_{t_1},\ldots,X_{t_r}).$$
This condition concerns the full finite-dimensional laws and imposes no moment
condition by itself.

The process is **weakly stationary** when $E[|X_t|^2]<\infty$ for every
$t\in\mathbb Z$, its mean $\mu:=E[X_t]$ is independent of $t$, and for every
$h\in\mathbb Z$ the covariance
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t)$$
is independent of $t$. Expectation, variance, and covariance have the meanings
in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Strict stationarity alone therefore
does not supply the moment hypotheses needed for covariance or sample-mean
claims.

For a weakly stationary real process $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$, its
**autocovariance function** (ACVF) is
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t),\qquad h\in\mathbb Z,$$
which is independent of $t$ by [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]].

For a finite data vector $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R$, where $n\ge1$, let
$$\bar x_n:=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n x_t.$$
Its **biased sample ACVF** is the zero-extended sequence on $\mathbb Z$ given by
$$\widehat\gamma_n(h):=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and $\widehat\gamma_n(h):=0$ for $|h|\ge n$. The absolute lag makes
$\widehat\gamma_n(-h)=\widehat\gamma_n(h)$.

For comparison, define the **pair-count-normalized rescaling**
$$\widetilde\gamma_n(h):=\frac1{n-|h|}\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and set it to zero for $|h|\ge n$. Its denominator is positive on the stated
domain. The names specify the denominator convention; they assert no
unbiasedness formula.

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Since weak stationarity gives $X_{n+h},Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\in L^2$, [F1] supplies a unique minimizing class and [F2] an affine representative with coefficients satisfying the normal equations. Every variable has mean $\mu$ by [F3], so the intercept is $a_0=\mu(1-\sum_i a_i)$ and the representative is $\mu+\sum_i a_i(Y_i-\mu)$.

For each $i,j$, the lag difference between $Y_i$ and $Y_j$ is $j-i$; covariance symmetry in [F5] gives $\gamma(j-i)=\gamma(i-j)$, so $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)=\Gamma_{ij}$. The lag from $Y_i=X_{n+1-i}$ to $X_{n+h}$ is $h+i-1$, so $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{n+h},Y_i)=\gamma(h+i-1)$. Rewriting step 1.1's equations gives $\Gamma a=\gamma_h$.
Under the statement's nonsingularity hypothesis, $\Gamma a=\gamma_h$ has the unique solution $a=\Gamma^{-1}\gamma_h$.

Put $U=X_{n+h}-\mu$ and $Z_i=Y_i-\mu$; the intercept equation makes the error mean zero, and stationarity gives $\mathbb E[UZ_i]=\gamma(h+i-1)$ and $\mathbb E[Z_iZ_j]=\Gamma_{ij}$. Expanding gives $\mathbb E[(U-a^TZ)^2]=\gamma(0)-2a^T\gamma_h+a^T\Gamma a=\gamma(0)-a^T\gamma_h$ because $\Gamma a=\gamma_h$. By [F6] this is the error variance.

vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The

Assume AC for existence. For real $X\in L^1(P)$, if $X$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[X\mid\mathcal G]=X$. If $P(\{X\in B\}\cap A)=P(X\in B)P(A)$ for every real Borel $B$ and $A\in\mathcal G$, then $E[X\mid\mathcal G]=EX$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.
If $Y,Z$ are conditional-expectation versions of the same real integrable $X$ given $\mathcal G$, then $Y=Z$ almost surely.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. derivations.claim: Let $Y=(X_n,\ldots,X_1)$ and choose an affine representative $\widehat X_{n+h}$ of the unique class in [F1]. Put $R=X_{n+h}-\widehat X_{n+h}$. By [F2], its mean is zero by the intercept equation, and each normal equation gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X_{n+h},Y_i)=\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat X_{n+h},Y_i)$, hence $\operatorname{Cov}(R,Y_i)=0$.

The vector $(R,Y)$ is an affine linear image of $(X_{n+h},Y)$, so every scalar linear projection is normal by [F3] and $(R,Y)$ is jointly multivariate normal. Step 1.1 gives zero cross-covariance between $R$ and each coordinate of $Y$, so [F4] makes $R$ independent of $Y$ and therefore of $\mathcal G:=\sigma(Y)$.

The forecast $\widehat X_{n+h}$ is an affine function of $Y$, hence $\mathcal G$-measurable and integrable. By [F5], $\mathbb E[R\mid\mathcal G]=\mathbb E[R]=0$ and $\mathbb E[\widehat X_{n+h}\mid\mathcal G]=\widehat X_{n+h}$. Since $X_{n+h}=R+\widehat X_{n+h}$, [F6] makes the forecast a version of $\mathbb E[X_{n+h}\mid\mathcal G]$ under [F7]; uniqueness in [F6] gives the almost-sure equality. AC is used only through the Gaussian and conditional-expectation branches.

**Input:** An integer $m\ge1$ and the lags $\gamma(0),\ldots,\gamma(m)$ of
the autocovariance function of a weakly stationary real process. Set
$\gamma(-r)=\gamma(r)$. Require every leading covariance matrix
$\Gamma_k=(\gamma(i-j))_{i,j=1}^k$ to be positive definite for $1\le k\le m$.

**Output:** Coefficient vectors $\phi_k=(\phi_{k,1},\ldots,\phi_{k,k})^T$
and error-variance values $\nu_k$ for $1\le k\le m$.

**Instructions:** Set $\nu_0=\gamma(0)$,
$\kappa_1=\gamma(1)/\nu_0$, $\phi_{1,1}=\kappa_1$, and
$\nu_1=\nu_0(1-\kappa_1^2)$. For each $k=2,\ldots,m$, set
$\kappa_k=[\gamma(k)-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\phi_{k-1,j}\gamma(k-j)]/\nu_{k-1}$,
$\phi_{k,j}=\phi_{k-1,j}-\kappa_k\phi_{k-1,k-j}$ for $1\le j<k$,
$\phi_{k,k}=\kappa_k$, and $\nu_k=\nu_{k-1}(1-\kappa_k^2)$.
Return all vectors and variances. The positive-definite leading-block
assumption makes each division well-defined; this is proved in
[[thm-durbin-levinson-solves-the-prediction-equations]]. The procedure operates
on covariance input and makes no Gaussian or conditional-expectation claim.

Let $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a weakly stationary real process with mean
$\mu$ and autocovariance $\gamma$, and let $n,h\ge1$. Define
$Y_i:=X_{n+1-i}$, $\Gamma_{ij}:=\gamma(i-j)$, and
$\gamma_h:=(\gamma(h),\gamma(h+1),\ldots,\gamma(h+n-1))^T$. If $\Gamma$ is
nonsingular, the unique forecast coefficients satisfy $a=\Gamma^{-1}\gamma_h$,
the best linear forecast is $\widehat X_{n+h}=\mu+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i(Y_i-\mu)$,
and its error variance is $\operatorname{Var}(X_{n+h}-\widehat X_{n+h})=\gamma(0)-a^T\gamma_h$.

For a weakly stationary real process $X=(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$, its
**autocovariance function** (ACVF) is
$$\gamma(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(X_{t+h},X_t),\qquad h\in\mathbb Z,$$
which is independent of $t$ by [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]].

For a finite data vector $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R$, where $n\ge1$, let
$$\bar x_n:=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n x_t.$$
Its **biased sample ACVF** is the zero-extended sequence on $\mathbb Z$ given by
$$\widehat\gamma_n(h):=\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and $\widehat\gamma_n(h):=0$ for $|h|\ge n$. The absolute lag makes
$\widehat\gamma_n(-h)=\widehat\gamma_n(h)$.

For comparison, define the **pair-count-normalized rescaling**
$$\widetilde\gamma_n(h):=\frac1{n-|h|}\sum_{t=1}^{n-|h|}(x_{t+|h|}-\bar x_n)(x_t-\bar x_n),\qquad |h|<n,$$
and set it to zero for $|h|\ge n$. Its denominator is positive on the stated
domain. The names specify the denominator convention; they assert no
unbiasedness formula.

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.

derivations.claim: For $k=1$, positive definiteness of $\Gamma_1=[\gamma(0)]$ gives $\gamma(0)>0$. The algorithm sets $\phi_{1,1}=\gamma(1)/\gamma(0)$, so $\Gamma_1\phi_1=r_1$, and [F2] gives error variance $\gamma(0)-\gamma(1)^2/\gamma(0)=\nu_1$, including the zero-error case.

For the induction step fix $2\le k\le m$ and assume the claim at order $k-1$. Write $r=(\gamma(1),\ldots,\gamma(k-1))^T$; covariance symmetry gives $\Gamma_k=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma(0)&r^T\\r&\Gamma_{k-1}\end{pmatrix}$. The induction hypothesis gives $\phi_{k-1}=\Gamma_{k-1}^{-1}r$ and $\nu_{k-1}=\gamma(0)-r^T\Gamma_{k-1}^{-1}r$. The positive quadratic form of $\Gamma_k$ at $(1,-\Gamma_{k-1}^{-1}r)^T$ equals this value, so $\nu_{k-1}>0$ and the order-$k$ division is valid.

Set $T=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\phi_{k-1,j}\gamma(k-j)$ and $\kappa_k=(\gamma(k)-T)/\nu_{k-1}$. For $i<k$, the new coefficient rule gives $(\Gamma_k\phi_k)_i=\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\gamma(i-j)\phi_{k-1,j}-\kappa_k\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\gamma(i-j)\phi_{k-1,k-j}+\kappa_k\gamma(i-k)$. The first sum is $\gamma(i)$ by the old system; reindexing the second by $\ell=k-j$ gives its row $k-i$, namely $\gamma(k-i)$. Since $\gamma(i-k)=\gamma(k-i)$, these last terms cancel and $(\Gamma_k\phi_k)_i=\gamma(i)$.

Let $S=r^T\phi_{k-1}=\gamma(0)-\nu_{k-1}$. Reindexing the last row gives $\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\gamma(k-j)\phi_{k-1,j}-\kappa_k\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\gamma(k-j)\phi_{k-1,k-j}+\kappa_k\gamma(0)=T+\kappa_k(\gamma(0)-S)=T+\kappa_k\nu_{k-1}=\gamma(k)$. Thus $\Gamma_k\phi_k=r_k$, and positive definiteness makes the solution unique.

Reindexing the new vector gives $r_k^T\phi_k=S-\kappa_kT+\kappa_k\gamma(k)=S+\kappa_k^2
u_{k-1}$ by the definition of $\kappa_k$. Therefore $\gamma(0)-r_k^T\phi_k=
u_{k-1}(1-\kappa_k^2)=
u_k$. The forecast theorem [F2] identifies this with the one-step projection-error variance, completing the induction through $k=m$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is

The values of $(X_1,X_2)$ at $\omega=0,1,2$ are $(-1,0),(0,1),(1,-1)$; hence both means are zero, $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=2/3$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X_2,X_1)=-1/3$. By [F4], the unique best affine forecast from this one-variable history is $(-1/3)/(2/3)X_1=-X_1/2$.

The conditional-expectation definition and known-variable property give $\mathbb E[X_2\mid\sigma(X_1)]=X_2$, whose values $(0,1,-1)$ differ from the affine forecast values $(1/2,0,-1/2)$ at every outcome.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: Reindexing the convergent causal series gives $X_t-\mu=\phi(X_{t-1}-\mu)+\epsilon_t$; repeating this identity gives $X_{n+h}-\mu=\phi^h(X_n-\mu)+R_h$, where $R_h=\sum_{r=0}^{h-1}\phi^r\epsilon_{n+h-r}$. Every innovation in $R_h$ has index greater than $n$, while the causal series for each $X_j-\mu$, $1\le j\le n$, uses only indices at most $j$.

For each $j\le n$, every finite partial sum for $X_j-\mu$ uses innovation indices at most $j$, so its covariance with each future term of $R_h$ is zero by the uncorrelated-noise assumption; [F4] passes this covariance identity to the $L^2$ limit. Thus $\operatorname{Cov}(R_h,X_j)=0$ and $\mathbb E[R_h]=0$, making the residual orthogonal to the constant and every history variable.

Let $H=\mu+\phi^h(X_n-\mu)$ and let any competing affine forecast $Z$ be in the history span; then $D:=H-Z$ is also in that span. Step 2.1 gives $\mathbb E[R_h]=0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(R_h,X_j)=0$ for every $j$; bilinearity [F3] gives $\operatorname{Cov}(R_h,D)=0$, hence $\mathbb E[R_hD]=0$. Since $X_{n+h}-Z=R_h+D$, expansion yields $\mathbb E[(X_{n+h}-Z)^2]=\mathbb E[R_h^2]+\mathbb E[D^2]\ge\mathbb E[R_h^2]$, with equality exactly when $D=0$ as an $L^2$ class. Thus $H$ is the unique best class by [F2]. The innovations in $R_h$ are pairwise uncorrelated, so [F3] gives $\operatorname{Var}(R_h)=\sigma^2\sum_{r=0}^{h-1}\phi^{2r}$. This proves both formulas without Gaussian or independent innovations.
